title: Where a company lives: incorporation, residence, management and control
summary: A company has a place of birth, which is where it was incorporated, and a tax home, which can be somewhere else. Where its real decisions are made can decide which country taxes it.
body:
Bottom line. A company is born in one place, but for tax it can live somewhere else. Mr Shabazz, the country that taxes a company usually depends on where it was incorporated and where its real decisions are made, so the location of your board meetings is a tax decision, not just a travel decision.

In plain English

Incorporation is the legal act that creates a company under a particular law. A company incorporated under the law of Alberta, or under the federal Canada Business Corporations Act, was born in Canada. A company incorporated in Guyana was born in Guyana. Its birthplace decides which corporate law governs its shareholders, directors and records.

Residence is a tax idea. It decides which country can tax the company on its worldwide income, rather than only on income earned inside that country. A company can be resident in more than one country at once, which is why tax treaties have rules to break the tie.

Central management and control is a test courts use for residence. It asks where the people who make the high-level decisions actually make them. It looks at reality, not at what the documents say.

The framework

Ask four questions, in this order.

  1. Where was it incorporated? Under subsection 250(4) of the Income Tax Act (Canada), a corporation incorporated in Canada after April 26, 1965 is deemed to be resident in Canada. So a Canadian-born company is resident in Canada for Canadian tax, whatever else is true.
  2. Where is it managed and controlled? Under the common law test from De Beers Consolidated Mines v Howe (House of Lords, 1906), which Canadian courts follow, a company is resident where its central management and control actually abides. A company born abroad can still be resident in Canada if its board really decides things from Canada.
  3. What does the other country say? Guyana and other countries have their own residence rules, which may look at incorporation, management, or both. Learn those rules from a local advisor. [unverified — confirm independently]
  4. Does a treaty break the tie? If two countries both claim the company, a tax treaty between them may decide which one wins. Many older treaties use place of effective management. Newer ones often leave it to the two tax authorities to agree.

Then look at the evidence of where control happens:

  • Where board meetings are held and where directors are physically present.
  • Where directors live, and whether local directors actually decide or only sign.
  • Where contracts are negotiated and signed, and where the bank accounts are run.
  • Whether one shareholder abroad really gives the orders, whatever the minutes say.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A Canadian developer sets up a company in Guyana to own a local project. The Guyanese company has three directors: two local professionals and the developer, who lives in Alberta. The minutes say every board meeting is held in Georgetown.

In practice, the developer decides every major question by email from Calgary, including a hypothetical $2,000,000 construction contract, and the two local directors sign whatever he sends. A Canadian tax auditor who reads the emails could argue that central management and control is in Canada. If that argument succeeds, the Guyanese company could be treated as resident in Canada and taxed in Canada on its worldwide income, while Guyana also taxes it as a local company. The treaty, if one applies, may or may not resolve the overlap. [unverified — confirm independently]

A cleaner approach is to give the local directors real authority, hold genuine board meetings in Guyana with the papers sent in advance, have the developer travel or attend in a way the advisors approve, and keep the decisions, the debate and the signatures there.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (cross-border, both countries) and corporate lawyer

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is believing that the place of incorporation settles the question. It settles corporate law, and in Canada it settles residence for Canadian-born companies. It does not stop a foreign-born company from being resident where it is really run. The second mistake is having local directors who are directors in name only. Courts look past the paper to the people who actually decide.

How you will use it

As a developer working across borders, treat the location of decisions as part of the structure. Before you form a foreign company, decide with your advisors where it should be resident and write a short governance protocol: where meetings happen, who attends, how papers are circulated, and which decisions the local board must make. Keep travel records and meeting packs. When you send instructions by email, remember that the email itself is evidence of where control lies. If you want control from Canada, plan for Canadian residence from the start. If you want the company resident abroad, let the people abroad genuinely decide.
checklist: Record where each company is incorporated and under which law
Decide, with advice, where each company should be tax resident
Write a governance protocol stating where board meetings happen
Appoint local directors who can and do make real decisions
Keep meeting papers, attendance and travel records
Check whether a tax treaty covers the two countries involved
Review email habits that could show control from another country

selftest.q: A company is incorporated in Guyana, but its only real decision-maker lives in Alberta and approves every contract from there. Which country might treat it as resident, and why?
selftest.a: Guyana may treat it as resident because it was incorporated there, subject to its own rules. Canada may treat it as resident under the central management and control test, because the real decisions are made in Alberta. That creates a risk of dual residence, which a treaty tie-breaker may or may not resolve.

apply: For any company you control, write one line saying where its last three major decisions were actually made and by whom.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada), subsection 250(4). De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd v Howe, House of Lords, 1906, on central management and control. Guyana residence rules and any Canada–Guyana treaty tie-breaker are tagged unverified; confirm with qualified advisors in each country. Education only, not advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (cross-border, both countries) and corporate lawyer

title: Stacking entities across borders: what each layer buys
summary: A cross-border structure is a stack of entities, and each layer should earn its place by buying liability protection, tax efficiency, financing flexibility or a cleaner exit. A layer that buys nothing only adds cost and risk.
body:
Bottom line. Every company in a cross-border structure should have a written reason to exist. Mr Shabazz, a layer can buy liability protection, tax efficiency, financing room or an easier sale, but each one also costs fees, filings and new rules, so add a layer only when you can name what it buys.

In plain English

A stack is a chain of ownership. You might own a Canadian holding company, which owns a foreign holding company, which owns a local operating company that owns the project. Each box is a separate legal person, so each one can hold its own assets, sign its own contracts and carry its own debts.

Three terms help. A subsidiary is a company owned by another company. A branch is not a separate company at all. It is an office or business that a company runs directly in another country. A special purpose vehicle, often called an SPV, is a company formed for one project only, so lenders and partners can see exactly what it owns and owes.

The framework

For each layer, test it against five things it might buy.

  1. Liability protection. A separate company can keep one project's lawsuits and debts away from other projects and from the owners, within the limits of corporate law and any guarantees signed.
  2. Financing. Lenders often want a clean SPV that owns only the financed asset, so they can take security over its shares or its land without other creditors in the way.
  3. Exit. Selling the shares of a holding company can be simpler than selling land, though tax and local consent rules may still apply. [unverified — confirm independently]
  4. Tax. A layer can change who is taxed, where, and when, for example by changing how dividends flow or which treaty applies. This is also where anti-avoidance rules focus.
  5. Local rules. Some countries require local ownership, local directors or a local company to hold certain licences or land.

Then count the cost of each layer:

  • Formation fees, annual filings, audits, registered agents and local directors.
  • Bank accounts, signing authority and know-your-customer checks in each country.
  • Tax rules that look through or ignore layers that lack substance. Canada has specific rules about foreign holding structures, such as the foreign affiliate dumping rules in section 212.3 of the Income Tax Act (Canada), whose scope needs expert review. [unverified — confirm independently]
  • Complexity for lenders and buyers, who must understand every box before they sign.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A developer plans a hypothetical $10,000,000 project in Guyana with a local partner. Option A: his Canadian holding company owns 60 percent of a Guyanese project company directly. Option B: his Canadian holding company owns an intermediate holding company in a third country, which owns 60 percent of the Guyanese company.

The advisors compare them. Option A has fewer filings and is easier for a Guyanese lender to understand. Option B might offer a better treaty on dividends or a more flexible law for a shareholders agreement, but it adds a third country's fees, audits and tax rules. It also invites a question from both tax authorities: does the middle company have real substance, such as staff, an office and decisions, or is it only a mailbox?

The advisors conclude that the middle layer buys a small and uncertain saving at a certain cost of about a hypothetical $40,000 a year, plus anti-avoidance risk. They recommend Option A, with the Guyanese company as an SPV owning only this project so the lender can take security cleanly.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (international) and corporate lawyers in each country

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is copying a structure because another developer used it, or because a diagram looked sophisticated. A layer in a low-tax country with no staff, no office and no decisions is the easiest kind for a tax authority to challenge. The second mistake is forgetting that every layer needs its own minute book, bank account, accounts and filings, forever, until it is wound up properly.

How you will use it

As a developer, draw the stack on one page before anyone forms a company. Next to each box, write one sentence saying what it buys and one saying what it costs each year. Ask your advisors to cross out any box whose sentence is weak. Also write down who will run each company, where its records will be kept, and who signs for it. A stack you can explain in two minutes to a lender is usually a stack that will survive a tax review. A stack you cannot explain is a warning sign, whoever designed it. Finally, plan the exit from each layer as well as the entry. Winding up a foreign company properly can take a year or more, with final audits, tax clearances and deregistration. A layer that is easy to create and hard to remove should be created only when its benefit is clear and lasting.
checklist: Draw the full ownership chain on one page
Write what each layer buys in one sentence
Estimate each layer's yearly cost in fees, audits and filings
Confirm each foreign layer can show real substance if asked
Check local ownership and licensing rules in each country
Ask whether a simpler stack achieves the same goals
Name who runs, keeps records for, and signs for each company

selftest.q: An advisor proposes adding a holding company in a third country between your Canadian holding company and a Guyanese project company. What questions should you ask before agreeing?
selftest.a: Ask what the layer buys in liability, financing, exit, tax or local compliance, and how much each benefit is worth. Ask what it costs each year, whether it will have real substance, which anti-avoidance rules in Canada and Guyana could ignore it, and whether lenders and buyers will accept it. If the benefit is small or uncertain, a simpler structure is usually better.

apply: Take one structure you use or are considering and write, beside each company, one line on what it buys and one on what it costs.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada), section 212.3 (foreign affiliate dumping), scope tagged unverified. Local ownership, consent and treaty points are tagged unverified and must be confirmed by advisors in each country. Education only, not advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor (international) and corporate lawyers in each country

title: Local content, beneficial ownership and look-through rules
summary: Many governments want to know who really owns a company, and some reward or require local participation. Look-through rules ignore the paper owner and trace ownership to the real people at the top.
body:
Bottom line. Regulators and banks increasingly ignore the name on the share register and ask which real people own and control a company. Mr Shabazz, if a structure depends on looking local or looking small, assume someone will trace it to the top, and design it so the true answer is acceptable.

In plain English

A legal owner is the person or company whose name is on the share register. A beneficial owner is the real person who ultimately owns, controls or benefits from the company, even if a nominee, a trust or a chain of companies sits in between. A nominee is someone who holds shares or a directorship in their own name for someone else.

Look-through rules are rules that ignore intermediate entities and trace ownership up the chain to real people. Local content rules are laws that require or reward the use of local companies, local workers, local suppliers or local owners in certain industries.

The framework

Expect four kinds of rule, and check each one in each country you work in.

  1. Beneficial ownership registers. In Canada, corporations under the Canada Business Corporations Act must keep a register of individuals with significant control, under section 21.1 of that Act, and federal reforms have moved toward a searchable public registry. Alberta has its own requirement for provincial corporations. [unverified — confirm independently] Guyana also has beneficial ownership requirements for companies. [unverified — confirm independently]
  2. Bank and anti-money-laundering checks. Banks, lawyers and real estate professionals must identify the beneficial owners of a client before acting. Expect to show passports, ownership charts and trust deeds.
  3. Local content and local ownership. Guyana has a Local Content Act, passed in 2021, which sets requirements for certain sectors, especially petroleum, and uses definitions of a Guyanese company and Guyanese national. Whether and how it applies to a real estate or construction business must be checked. [unverified — confirm independently]
  4. Tax look-through. Tax rules often count ownership through chains of companies and trusts to decide whether entities are related, associated or controlled. Canada's rules on associated corporations and control, for example, look through trusts and nominees. The details are complex.

For each rule, ask three questions:

  • What percentage or kind of control triggers the rule?
  • Does it look through trusts, nominees and holding companies?
  • What happens if the filing is wrong or late: a fine, a lost licence, or a voided contract?

A worked example

This example is hypothetical. A Guyanese company bids for a contract that gives preference to companies with majority local ownership. On paper, 51 percent of its shares are held by a Guyanese individual and 49 percent by the developer's Canadian holding company.

But the Guyanese individual signed a side agreement promising to vote as the developer directs and to pass all dividends to him, in exchange for a hypothetical $20,000 a year fee. That individual is a nominee. The developer is the beneficial owner of the 51 percent as well.

If the contract's local ownership test looks through to beneficial owners, the company does not qualify, and the bid may have been a false declaration. If a bank's beneficial ownership form listed only the nominee, the developer may have made a false statement to the bank. The cost of discovery could be losing the contract, penalties, and reputational damage with every lender in the market.

A lawful approach is a real partnership: a local partner who invests real money, takes real risk, votes independently and receives real returns, documented in a shareholders agreement both sides can show to anyone.

Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate lawyer in the host country and compliance advisor

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is treating a nominee as a clever workaround. In many systems a nominee arrangement that hides the true owner from a regulator, a bank or a contracting authority is unlawful in itself, separate from whatever it was meant to achieve. The second mistake is forgetting to update registers when ownership changes. A register that was true last year may be false today.

How you will use it

As a developer, keep one living ownership chart for every company you touch, showing legal owners, beneficial owners, trusts and percentages, with the date it was last checked. Give it to your lawyer before you form a company, open an account or bid for a contract that has ownership conditions. When a local partner is needed, choose a partner who genuinely invests and decides, and pay them for that, not for their name. Assume every chain will one day be traced to the top, and make sure the answer at the top is one you are comfortable showing. When a bank or lawyer asks for beneficial ownership information, answer it fully and keep a copy of what you gave them. Different answers to different institutions are a common way problems surface, because these records are compared more often than most people expect.
checklist: Keep a dated ownership chart showing legal and beneficial owners
Confirm each company's beneficial ownership register is current
Check whether any contract, licence or incentive has an ownership test
Read how that test treats trusts, nominees and holding companies
Never use a nominee to hide the true owner from a regulator or bank
Document any local partner's real investment, risk and independent vote
Update registers and bank records within the deadline after any change

selftest.q: A local director holds 51 percent of the shares but has signed a private agreement to vote as you instruct and pass you the dividends. A contract requires majority local ownership. What is the problem?
selftest.a: The local director is a nominee and you are the beneficial owner of the 51 percent. If the contract or regulator looks through to beneficial ownership, the company does not qualify, and any declaration that it does could be false. Similar issues arise with bank and register filings. The arrangement creates legal and reputational risk.

apply: Draw a dated ownership chart for one company you control, showing every legal owner and every real person behind them.
sources: Canada Business Corporations Act, section 21.1 (register of individuals with significant control). Alberta's equivalent requirement, the federal public registry details, Guyana's beneficial ownership rules and the Local Content Act 2021 of Guyana are tagged unverified; confirm the current text with counsel in each jurisdiction. Education only, not advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate lawyer in the host country and compliance advisor

title: Repatriating money: dividends, loans, fees and leakage
summary: Getting profit home from another country can happen through dividends, loan repayments, interest or fees, and each route carries different taxes and costs. The money lost along the way is called leakage, and good planning measures it before money moves.
body:
Bottom line. Earning money in another country is only half the job; bringing it home is the other half. Mr Shabazz, each route home, whether a dividend, a loan repayment, interest or a fee, loses a different slice to withholding tax, income tax, currency costs and bank charges, so compare the routes before the money is earned, not after.

In plain English

Repatriation means moving money from a foreign company back to its owners in the home country. Leakage is everything lost on the way: taxes in the foreign country, taxes at home, currency exchange spreads, and fees.

Withholding tax is tax that the paying country takes from a payment to a non-resident before the money leaves. The payer deducts it and sends it to its government. Canada's version, for payments from Canada to non-residents, is in Part XIII of the Income Tax Act (Canada); section 212 sets a general rate of 25 percent, which a tax treaty may reduce. Payments from Guyana to Canada are subject to Guyana's own withholding rules. [unverified — confirm independently]

The framework

Compare the four main routes.

  1. Dividends. The foreign company pays tax on its profit, then pays a dividend. The foreign country may withhold tax on the dividend. In Canada, dividends from a foreign affiliate to a Canadian corporation may be largely deductible depending on the affiliate's surplus accounts, which lesson 35 covers.
  2. Return of capital and loan repayments. Paying back money the owner put in is usually not income to the owner. That is why many structures put part of the investment in as a loan. The foreign country may limit how much of a company's funding can be debt.
  3. Interest. Interest on a real loan may be deductible to the foreign company, lowering its tax, but it may face withholding and is taxable to the Canadian lender. Rules against excessive related-party debt, often called thin capitalization rules, can deny the deduction. [unverified — confirm independently]
  4. Fees and charges. Management, technical or licence fees for real services can also move money and may be deductible abroad. They must reflect real services at a fair price. Canada's transfer pricing rules in section 247 of the Income Tax Act (Canada), and the other country's equivalents, require arm's length prices between related parties.

Then check three cross-cutting points:

  • Foreign tax credits. Canada may give a credit for foreign tax paid on income it also taxes, under section 126, which reduces double tax but rarely removes it perfectly.
  • Currency. Exchange spreads and timing can cost more than a percentage point of tax.
  • Exchange controls and banking. Some countries restrict or slow outbound payments, and banks may hold payments for review.

A worked example

This example is hypothetical, and every rate in it is made up for illustration. A Guyanese project company has a hypothetical $1,000,000 of after-tax cash to send to its Canadian owner.

Route 1, a dividend: suppose a hypothetical 10 percent withholding applies, so $100,000 stays in Guyana. Currency and bank costs take a hypothetical $15,000. The Canadian holding company receives $885,000, and its Canadian tax depends on the surplus rules.

Route 2, repaying a documented shareholder loan: suppose no withholding applies to a repayment of principal. Costs take $15,000, so $985,000 arrives. But this only works up to the amount genuinely lent, and only if the loan was properly documented when made.

The lesson is not that loans are always better. It is that the funding choice made on day one, debt or shares, decides which routes exist years later. The advisors build a table showing each route's leakage under the real rules before the project is funded.

Professional Sign-Off Required: international tax advisor (both countries) and banking or treasury advisor

The beginner mistake

The beginner mistake is funding a foreign project entirely with share capital, then discovering that every dollar coming home must be a dividend with withholding. The second mistake is inventing a management fee with no real services behind it. Tax authorities on both sides can deny the deduction, recharacterize the payment, and add penalties.

How you will use it

As a developer, decide the repatriation plan at the same meeting where you decide the funding. Ask your advisors for a one-page table: each route, the tax in each country, currency cost, timing, and conditions. Document every loan with a signed agreement, interest terms and a repayment schedule. If fees will be charged, keep evidence of the real services. Revisit the table each year, because rates, treaties and banking practices change. Finally, remember that the cheapest route on paper is not always the right one. A route that saves a little tax but takes months to clear the bank, or that depends on an aggressive reading of a treaty, may cost more in delay and risk than it saves. Ask your advisor to rate each route for certainty as well as for cost, and choose the one you could defend calmly in an audit.
checklist: Decide the mix of share capital and loans before funding a foreign company
Ask for a table of leakage by route, in each country
Document every intercompany loan with signed terms and schedule
Charge fees only for real services, with evidence and fair prices
Check foreign withholding rates and any treaty reduction
Plan currency conversion and banking timelines
Review the repatriation plan every year

selftest.q: You funded a foreign project company entirely with shares. It now has surplus cash. Why might you wish you had used a mix of shares and a documented loan?
selftest.a: With only share capital, cash usually comes home as dividends, which may face foreign withholding tax and other costs. A properly documented loan could have allowed part of the cash to come home as a repayment of principal, which often has little or no withholding, subject to thin capitalization and transfer pricing rules in both countries.

apply: For any foreign or planned foreign company, write how the first dollar of profit would come home and list each tax or cost it would meet on the way.
sources: Income Tax Act (Canada): section 212 (Part XIII withholding, general 25 percent rate), section 247 (transfer pricing), section 126 (foreign tax credit). Guyana withholding rates, thin capitalization rules and any Canada–Guyana treaty rates are tagged unverified. All rates in the example are hypothetical. Education only, not advice.
signoff: Professional Sign-Off Required: international tax advisor (both countries) and banking or treasury advisor
